docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text: Zero-trust architectures need workload identity that doesn't depend on network location, IP allowlists, or shared secrets. SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework For Everyone) defines the identity standard; SPIRE is the reference implementation. Together they let services prove who they are using cryptographic identities issued automatically based on platform attestation — no API keys to rotate, no certs to manage, mTLS that "just works" across clusters and clouds.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Every workload gets a SPIFFE ID (a URI like spiffe://acme.com/payments/api). The platform proves what the workload is via attestation (k8s pod metadata, AWS instance identity doc, etc.), and SPIRE issues a short-lived SVID (SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document) — either x509 (for mTLS) or JWT (for API calls). Workloads consume SVIDs over a local Unix socket — they never see private keys cross the network.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Workload] -->|asks for SVID via Workload API| B[SPIRE Agentper node]
    B -->|attest workloadUID, k8s labels, etc| B
    B -->|already attested by SPIRE Server| C[SPIRE Server]
    C -->|signs SVID matchingregistration entry| B
    B -->|hand SVID to workload| A
    A -->|use SVID for mTLS| D[Other workload]
    D -->|verify SVID against trust bundle| D

docs.title: SPIFFE Identity
docs.text:
spiffe://<trust-domain>/<workload-path>
        e.g. spiffe://acme.com/ns/prod/sa/payments-api
Part Meaning trust-domain Administrative boundary (org, team, cluster). Trust bundles are scoped here. workload-path Hierarchical, organization-defined. No reserved meaning. Common: /ns/<namespace>/sa/<service-account> for k8s.

Trust domains are equivalent to a CA's authority — workloads in the same trust domain implicitly trust the same root.

docs.title: SVID Forms
docs.text:
Form Format Use x509-SVID x509 cert with SPIFFE ID in URI SAN, plus private key mTLS — TLS handshake authenticates BOTH sides JWT-SVID JWT with sub = SPIFFE ID, signed by trust-domain key API auth where TLS is terminated upstream (e.g. behind a load balancer or for RPC headers)

Both are short-lived (typical default: 1 hour for x509, 5 min for JWT) and rotated automatically by SPIRE Agent before expiry.

Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[x509-SVID] --> B[Cert with SPIFFE IDin SAN URI]
    A --> C[Private key]
    A --> D[Trust bundlechain to SPIRE Server's CA]
    E[JWT-SVID] --> F[JWT: sub=SPIFFE ID,aud=target service]
    E --> G[JWKS to verifyfrom Workload API]

docs.title: SPIRE Architecture
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart TB
    SS[SPIRE Server1+ replicas, central CA] --> DS[(DatastorePostgres/MySQL/SQLite)]
    SS --- KS[KeyManagerdisk / AWS KMS / HSM]
    A1[SPIRE Agentnode 1] -.attested.-> SS
    A2[SPIRE Agentnode 2] -.attested.-> SS
    W1[Workload A] -->|Workload API socket| A1
    W2[Workload B] -->|Workload API socket| A1
    W3[Workload C] -->|Workload API socket| A2
Component Role SPIRE Server Root CA for the trust domain. Holds registration entries (rules: "if X, issue SPIFFE ID Y"). Signs SVIDs. SPIRE Agent Runs on every node (DaemonSet on k8s). Attests itself to Server, then attests local workloads and proxies SVIDs. Workload API gRPC API exposed via a Unix domain socket (/run/spire/agent.sock). Workloads call FetchX509SVID / FetchJWTSVID. Registration Entries Rules in Server's datastore: selectors (k8s label, AWS instance tag, Unix UID) → SPIFFE ID to issue.

docs.title: Two-Stage Attestation
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
sequenceDiagram
    participant N as Node
    participant A as SPIRE Agent
    participant S as SPIRE Server
    participant W as Workload pod

    Note over N,S: Stage 1: Node attestation (once at boot)
    A->>N: Read attestation evidence(AWS IID, k8s PSAT, x509)
    A->>S: Connect with evidence
    S->>S: Verify evidence with NodeAttestor plugin
    S-->>A: Issue Agent SVID

    Note over W,A: Stage 2: Workload attestation (per fetch)
    W->>A: gRPC FetchX509SVID via UDS
    A->>A: Get caller PID from socket
    A->>A: WorkloadAttestor plugins:k8s label, Unix UID, Docker label
    A->>A: Match selectors to registration entries
    A->>S: Request SVID for matched SPIFFE ID
    S-->>A: x509-SVID + key + bundle
    A-->>W: SVID material

The two-stage model means: a compromised workload cannot impersonate another, because the AGENT (not the workload) proves identity using kernel-level data the workload can't forge (PID → cgroup → k8s pod → labels).

docs.title: Annotated Registration Entry
docs.text:
# Register that any pod in namespace "prod" with SA "payments-api"
# running on a node in the "us-east-1a" trust group gets this SPIFFE ID
spire-server entry create \
  -spiffeID spiffe://acme.com/ns/prod/sa/payments-api \
  -parentID spiffe://acme.com/spire/agent/k8s_psat/prod-cluster/abc123 \
  -selector k8s:ns:prod \
  -selector k8s:sa:payments-api \
  -selector k8s:pod-label:app:payments-api \
  -ttl 3600

Selectors are AND'd within an entry. A workload must satisfy ALL selectors for the entry to apply. Multiple entries can apply — workload gets multiple SVIDs.

docs.title: mTLS Without Secrets
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Service A
    participant SA as SPIRE Agent A
    participant B as Service B
    participant SB as SPIRE Agent B

    A->>SA: FetchX509SVID
    SA-->>A: SVID + key + trust bundle
    B->>SB: FetchX509SVID
    SB-->>B: SVID + key + trust bundle

    A->>B: TLS ClientHello
    B->>A: ServerHello + cert (B's SVID)
    A->>A: Verify cert against trust bundleextract SPIFFE ID from SAN
    A->>A: Authorize: is this the SPIFFE ID I expected?
    A->>B: Client cert (A's SVID)
    B->>B: Verify + extract SPIFFE ID + authorize
    A->>B: HTTP/2 traffic

Both sides authenticate AND authorize on SPIFFE ID, not on IP/hostname. Trust bundle is auto-rotated by the agent — if SPIRE Server rotates its CA, agents fetch the new bundle and push to workloads BEFORE old certs expire.

docs.title: Integration: Envoy SDS
docs.text: Envoy fetches SVIDs via the SPIFFE-flavored SDS (Secret Discovery Service). The application code doesn't change — Envoy sidecar terminates and originates mTLS using SPIRE-issued certs. This is how Istio (with --set values.global.spiffe.enabled) and Consul Connect can layer on SPIRE.

docs.title: Common Interview Questions
docs.text:
[!IMPORTANT] Q1: What is a SPIFFE ID? A: A URI of the form spiffe://<trust-domain>/<workload-path> that uniquely identifies a workload. It's embedded in the URI SAN of x509-SVIDs and the sub claim of JWT-SVIDs.

Q2: x509-SVID vs JWT-SVID — when to use which? A: x509-SVID for mTLS (TCP-level mutual auth between services). JWT-SVID for API auth where TLS is terminated upstream (load balancer) or for RPC headers / cross-cluster requests.

Q3: How does SPIRE attest a workload running in a pod? A: Two stages. First, the SPIRE Agent on the node attests ITSELF to the SPIRE Server via a NodeAttestor plugin (e.g. k8s PSAT, AWS IID). Then, when a workload calls the Workload API, the agent uses the caller PID to introspect cgroups → pod → labels/SA, and matches against registration entry selectors.

Q4: Why is mTLS with SPIRE "without secrets"? A: Workloads never see long-lived keys. SVIDs are issued per workload, short-lived (1h default), and rotated automatically. Compromise window is bounded; there's no API key to leak or rotate.

Q5: What's a trust domain and why does it matter? A: An administrative boundary (e.g. acme.com or prod.acme.com). Each trust domain has its own root CA. Workloads in the same trust domain implicitly trust each other. Cross-domain trust uses federation: each domain publishes its bundle for the other to trust selectively.

Q6: How does the Workload API prevent workload-to-workload impersonation? A: The agent identifies the caller via the Unix socket peer PID, then introspects kernel-level metadata (cgroups, namespaces) the workload can't forge. The workload doesn't tell the agent who it is — the agent observes.

Q7: What happens when SPIRE Server's CA needs to rotate? A: SPIRE Server generates a new CA, signs new SVIDs with it, and publishes both old and new in the trust bundle. Agents push the updated bundle to workloads. After all old SVIDs expire, the old CA is removed from the bundle. Zero downtime.

Q8: How is SPIRE different from a service mesh's mTLS? A: SPIRE is identity infrastructure; service meshes consume identities. Istio/Linkerd have built-in identity (Citadel/identity service) but they're mesh-scoped. SPIRE is mesh-independent, can identify non-mesh workloads (databases, edge functions, lambdas), and supports federation across clouds.

docs.title: Audit logging
docs.text:
The api-server's audit subsystem produces JSON events for every API call. Configure with --audit-policy-file and --audit-log-path (or webhook to SIEM).

See audit-policy.yaml — the canonical "log enough but not too much" policy.

Levels: - None — drop event - Metadata — request metadata only (who/what/when, not body) - Request — metadata + request body (no response) - RequestResponse — full body both ways

Rule of thumb: - Secrets / TokenReviews → Metadata (never log the body!) - Pods/exec/portforward → RequestResponse (forensics) - Read-only verbs on non-sensitive resources → None (volume control)

docs.title: Tooling
docs.text: Tool Use kube-bench CIS benchmark evidence Trivy / Grype Vuln scan reports Falco Runtime detection logs OPA Gatekeeper / Kyverno Policy attestation — every workload screened Open Policy Agent (general) Cross-system compliance evaluation Steampipe / CloudQuery Cloud config evidence Wiz / Lacework / Prisma Commercial CSPM with framework mappings

docs.title: Files
docs.text: • audit-policy.yaml — production-ready audit policy

docs.title: Practical tips
docs.text:
1. Automate evidence: every report should be reproducible from a script. Manual screenshots = audit hell.
  2. Treat policies as code: every Kyverno/Gatekeeper policy is a control attestation.
  3. Pre-stage scope: PCI/HIPAA workloads in dedicated clusters or namespaces with stricter controls — avoid scoping the entire org.
  4. Continuous, not point-in-time: SOC 2 Type 2 needs operating effectiveness over months, not one-off snapshots.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
# Audit policy on the API server
sudo cp audit-policy.yaml /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
sudo chmod 0600 /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml

# Wire into kube-apiserver static pod manifest
sudo vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml
# - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit.log
# - --audit-log-maxage=30
# - --audit-log-maxbackup=10
# - --audit-log-maxsize=100

# Compliance-friendly tools
brew install aquasecurity/trivy/trivy
docker pull aquasec/kube-bench:latest
helm install kyverno kyverno/kyverno -n kyverno --create-namespace
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace

docs.title: Apply policies / manifests
docs.text:
# CIS evidence (kube-bench Job)
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml

# Vulnerability evidence (Trivy operator continuously scans)
helm repo add aqua https://aquasecurity.github.io/helm-charts/
helm install trivy-operator aqua/trivy-operator \
  -n trivy-system --create-namespace

# Policy attestation (Kyverno produces PolicyReports — direct evidence)
kubectl apply -f /path/to/kyverno-baseline-policies/

docs.title: Inspect / verify
docs.text:
# Audit log — who did what
sudo tail -f /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | jq .

# Filter audit log for sensitive verbs on Secrets
sudo jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets" and .verb!="list")' \
  /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log

# CIS evidence
kubectl logs job.batch/kube-bench > cis-evidence-$(date +%F).txt

# CVE evidence
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A
kubectl get configauditreports -A
trivy k8s --report all cluster > vuln-evidence-$(date +%F).json

# Policy evidence
kubectl get policyreport -A -o json > policy-evidence-$(date +%F).json
kubectl get clusterpolicyreport -o json

# Falco runtime evidence (forward to S3/Splunk for retention)
kubectl logs -n falco -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco --since=24h > runtime-events.log

# Encryption-at-rest evidence
sudo grep encryption-provider-config /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

docs.title: Common operations
docs.text:
# RBAC review — every binding to admin / cluster-admin
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o json \
  | jq '.items[] | select(.roleRef.name | test("admin"))'

# NetworkPolicy coverage report
kubectl get netpol -A -o json \
  | jq '.items | group_by(.metadata.namespace) | map({ns: .[0].metadata.namespace, count: length})'

# mTLS coverage (Istio)
istioctl authn tls-check <pod>.<ns>

# Image signing coverage
for img in $(kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{..image}' | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u); do
  cosign verify "$img" \
    --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/org/.*' \
    --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
    >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "OK $img" || echo "UNSIGNED $img"
done

docs.text:
# Daily evidence collection script (cron-friendly)
DATE=$(date +%F); mkdir -p evidence/$DATE
kubectl logs job.batch/kube-bench > evidence/$DATE/cis.txt
kubectl get vulnerabilityreports -A -o json > evidence/$DATE/vulns.json
kubectl get policyreport -A -o json > evidence/$DATE/policies.json
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o yaml > evidence/$DATE/rbac.yaml

# Top-volume audit events (tune --audit-policy)
sudo jq -r '.objectRef.resource' /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

# Confirm secrets ARE logged at Metadata only (never RequestResponse)
sudo jq 'select(.objectRef.resource=="secrets") | .level' \
  /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log | sort -u

docs.title: Architect Q&A — Security
docs.text: 60+ Q&A for senior, staff, and architect-level Kubernetes and cloud-native security decisions. Covers multi-tenant boundaries, supply-chain SLSA L3 program, OIDC trust to cloud, secret rotation at scale, runtime detection at scale, zero-trust mesh adoption, compliance program design, and incident response playbooks.

docs.title: Q1. What is the strongest tenant boundary in Kubernetes?
docs.text: A separate cluster. Namespace isolation is a soft boundary — node, kernel, and control-plane are shared. For hostile multi-tenancy, use cluster-per-tenant or vCluster + node pool isolation + gVisor/Kata.

docs.title: Q2. When is namespace-per-tenant acceptable?
docs.text: Cooperative tenants (same company, internal teams). Enforce: NetworkPolicy default-deny, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, RBAC scoped to namespace, no shared CRDs that leak data, PSA restricted.

docs.title: Q3. How do you prevent a tenant from reading another tenant's secrets?
docs.text: RBAC scoped to namespace, no ClusterRoleBindings granting cross-namespace get on Secrets, encrypt-at-rest in etcd with KMS, audit on Secret access, External Secrets per-namespace SA with IRSA scoped to tenant prefix in the secret store.

docs.title: Q4. How do you stop tenants from consuming all node resources?
docs.text: ResourceQuota for cpu/memory/pods, LimitRange defaults, PriorityClass for system workloads, dedicated node pools per tier with taints + tolerations, scheduler with anti-affinity.

docs.title: Q5. What is vCluster and when do you pick it over namespaces?
docs.text: vCluster runs a virtual control plane inside a host namespace. Picks: tenants need cluster-admin for their own scope, want their own CRDs, version skew. Caveat: still shares host nodes — not a hard isolation boundary unless combined with sandbox runtime.

docs.title: Q6. How do you prevent privileged escalation across tenants?
docs.text: Pod Security Admission restricted on tenant namespaces, baseline on system, drop ALL caps, no hostPath, no hostNetwork, no privileged, seccomp RuntimeDefault, read-only root FS. Validate via Kyverno or Gatekeeper as belt-and-suspenders.

docs.title: Q7. How do you isolate tenant traffic east-west?
docs.text: Cilium with cluster-mesh and tenant labels; default-deny NetworkPolicy; per-tenant L7 policies for shared services; egress via per-tenant gateways; mTLS via mesh with SPIFFE IDs that encode tenant.

docs.title: Q8. How do you handle shared cluster-scoped resources like CRDs and webhooks?
docs.text: Platform team owns CRDs. Tenants get RBAC only on namespaced custom resources. Validating webhooks must be tenant-aware via namespace selectors. Conversion webhooks run with platform identity, not tenant.

docs.title: Q9. How do you prevent noisy neighbor in storage?
docs.text: Per-tenant StorageClass with IOPS/throughput limits, CSI quota, ceph/EBS namespace-scoped pools, monitor PVC consumption with quotas.

docs.title: Q10. What is the audit strategy for multi-tenant?
docs.text: Audit policy: log Metadata for all, RequestResponse for tenant Secret/ConfigMap writes. Stream to per-tenant index in SIEM. Retain 1 year. Tenants get read on their slice via API.

docs.title: Q11. What is SLSA L3 in one sentence?
docs.text: Builds run on a hardened, hosted, isolated builder that produces non-forgeable provenance signed by the platform.

docs.title: Q12. What are the L3 hard requirements?
docs.text: Hosted build platform (no self-hosted runners with mutable state), isolated build per invocation, parameterless build entry, hermetic where possible, signed provenance generated by the platform key.

docs.title: Q13. How do you reach L3 with GitHub Actions?
docs.text: Use GitHub-hosted runners (or actions-runner-controller with ephemeral pods), use the SLSA generic generator workflow, sign with sigstore keyless using the GitHub OIDC token, attach in-toto attestation to the OCI registry via cosign.

docs.title: Q14. How do you verify SLSA provenance at admission?
docs.text: Cosign policy controller or Kyverno verifyImages rule with the predicate type slsaprovenance and an issuer/subject regex matching your build platform's OIDC identity.

docs.title: Q15. Where do attestations live?
docs.text: As OCI artifacts referenced by digest in the same registry. cosign download attestation registry/app@sha256:... returns DSSE envelopes containing in-toto statements.

docs.title: Q16. How do you handle base image trust?
docs.text: Pin by digest. Rebuild base images in your own pipeline producing your own provenance. Mirror upstream into a private registry with a verification policy that requires either internal provenance or vendor signature.

docs.title: Q17. What is the rollout plan for SLSA L3 across 200 services?
docs.text: Phase 1: instrument top 10 critical services, pilot signing and verification in staging with --enforce=warn. Phase 2: enforce in staging, warn in prod, build dashboards. Phase 3: enforce in prod for tier 1, expand cohort by cohort. Phase 4: deny unsigned by default.

docs.title: Q18. What gets signed and what gets attested?
docs.text: Sign: container images, Helm charts, OCI artifacts. Attest: SBOM (cyclonedx/spdx), SLSA provenance, vulnerability scan results, test results, custom predicate types (e.g. internal review approval).

docs.title: Q19. How do you prevent dependency confusion?
docs.text: Private registry first in resolver config, scope locks, pin transitive deps, mirror approved deps only, block public installs in CI behind explicit allowlist.

docs.title: Q20. How do you handle SBOM at scale?
docs.text: Generate at build with syft, attach as attestation, push to a central SBOM store (DependencyTrack or Snyk), continuously scan against fresh CVE feeds, alert on new CVEs against deployed digests.

docs.title: Q21. Why use OIDC federation over static cloud keys for K8s workloads?
docs.text: No long-lived secrets in cluster, automatic rotation by IdP, fine-grained policies bound to the workload identity, audit on the cloud side.

docs.title: Q22. How does IRSA work in EKS?
docs.text: EKS issues OIDC tokens to ServiceAccounts. AWS IAM trusts the cluster's OIDC issuer URL. The pod's projected SA token is exchanged via STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. The workload assumes a role scoped via condition keys on sub matching system:serviceaccount:ns:sa.

docs.title: Q23. How do you trust GitHub Actions to deploy to AWS without a static key?
docs.text: Configure AWS IAM OIDC provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com. Create a role with trust policy conditioning on sub like repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main and aud=sts.amazonaws.com. Use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4.

docs.title: Q24. What is the equivalent for GCP?
docs.text: Workload Identity Federation. Create a workload identity pool, add provider with the OIDC issuer, bind a service account with principalSet://... condition.

docs.title: Q25. What is the equivalent for Azure?
docs.text: Azure Workload Identity for AKS, federated identity credentials on a managed identity referencing the OIDC issuer URL.

docs.title: Q26. How do you scope tokens minimally?
docs.text: Use audience claim restriction, short TTL (1h max), conditions on sub for exact SA, branch-or-tag restriction in CI, never wildcard repo:org/*.

docs.title: Q27. How do you rotate the cluster OIDC signing key?
docs.text: Managed services rotate automatically on EKS/AKS/GKE. For self-hosted, rotate kube-apiserver --service-account-signing-key-file with overlap window, publish JWKS, update IAM provider thumbprint if needed.

docs.title: Q28. What is the failure mode if OIDC issuer URL is wrong?
docs.text: Workloads cannot assume cloud roles, deployments stall on cloud calls. Mitigation: monitor STS errors, alert on AccessDenied spikes, runbook to verify OIDC provider thumbprint and issuer.

docs.title: Q29. How do you audit OIDC token usage?
docs.text: CloudTrail for AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity events, GCP audit logs for STS token exchanges, correlate on sub claim back to namespace/SA. Forward to SIEM.

docs.title: Q30. How do you prevent token replay across regions or environments?
docs.text: Audience claim per environment, short TTL, IP condition where possible, distinct OIDC issuer per cluster, IRSA roles per env with naming convention.

docs.title: Q31. What is the right secret store for K8s at scale?
docs.text: External Secrets Operator + Vault or AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager / Azure Key Vault. Vault wins for dynamic secrets (DB credentials), cloud-native wins for managed simplicity.

docs.title: Q32. How do you rotate a database password without downtime?
docs.text: Two-credential rotation: app uses cred A, rotate to B in store, ESO refreshes secret in K8s, app reloads (sidecar reloader or SIGHUP), invalidate A. Or use Vault dynamic DB secrets with short TTL and lease renewal.

docs.title: Q33. How do you rotate TLS certs at scale?
docs.text: cert-manager with ACME or internal CA, short-lived certs (24h to 90d), reloader watching Secret to roll Deployments, mesh handles workload certs automatically (Istio rotates SVID hourly).

docs.title: Q34. What is the strategy for static secrets that must rotate?
docs.text: Tag with TTL annotation, scheduled job to rotate via API to source store, ESO syncs, application reads via volume mount with subPath, app code retries on auth failure.

docs.title: Q35. How do you prove rotation happened?
docs.text: Audit log on store side, K8s event on Secret update, metric secret_age_seconds exposed by an exporter scraping Secret annotations, alert when > SLA.

docs.title: Q36. What about sealed-secrets — when is it appropriate?
docs.text: Small clusters, GitOps-only, no central store. Caveats: rotation requires re-sealing and committing, the sealing key is a single point of trust. Prefer ESO for anything beyond 10 services.

docs.title: Q37. How do you prevent a secret from being logged?
docs.text: Disable RequestResponse audit on Secrets, redact in app logs, lint pipelines for kubectl get secret -o yaml in scripts, use --token-only flags, ban env vars for highly sensitive secrets — prefer projected volumes.

docs.title: Q38. How do you handle secret access during a Vault outage?
docs.text: Cache last-known value in K8s Secret with ESO, set high refresh interval for non-critical, use Vault Performance Standby, consider regional Vault clusters with replication, fallback to read-only mode in app.

docs.title: Q39. How do you grant least privilege on the secret store?
docs.text: One Vault role per app per env, policies on path secret/data/env/app/*, K8s auth method binding SA to role, audit device on Vault streaming to SIEM, deny * policies.

docs.title: Q40. How do you onboard a new app to External Secrets?
docs.text: Template: Helm chart includes ExternalSecret and SecretStore ref, Vault path computed from {env}/{namespace}/{app}, SA bound to Vault role via Kubernetes auth, CI bootstraps the Vault role via Terraform on first deploy.

docs.title: Q41. Falco vs Tetragon — which to pick?
docs.text: Falco: rule-based, mature, kernel module or eBPF, alerts to falcosidekick. Tetragon: eBPF-native, in-kernel filtering and enforcement, lower overhead at high event volume. Use Tetragon for fleets > 500 nodes or where you need policy enforcement, Falco for mature alerting and community rules.

docs.title: Q42. What rules do you start with?
docs.text: Falco default rules + k8s_audit. Highest value: shell in container, write to /etc, mount of sensitive paths, outbound to non-allowlist destination, exec into kube-system, change to RBAC.

docs.title: Q43. How do you tune false positives?
docs.text: Macro overrides in falco_rules.local.yaml, exception lists per workload label, suppression at falcosidekick before SIEM, weekly review of fired rules with action: tune, delete, escalate.

docs.title: Q44. How do you ship events at scale?
docs.text: Falcosidekick to Kafka, downstream consumers: SIEM (Splunk/Elastic), enrichment service adding pod metadata, deduplication, alert manager. Avoid direct SIEM push from each node.

docs.title: Q45. What is the cardinality risk?
docs.text: Per-event labels (pod, image, command) explode metric cardinality. Use logs not metrics for events, keep metrics aggregated by rule + namespace.

docs.title: Q46. How do you enforce with Tetragon?
docs.text: TracingPolicy with enforcer action — kill, override return value, signal. Example: kill any process opening /etc/shadow outside allowlist. Roll out per-namespace.

docs.title: Q47. Detection coverage map?
docs.text: Map rules to MITRE ATT&CK for Containers. Track coverage per tactic. Aim for detection in: Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Defense Evasion, Credential Access, Discovery, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration.

docs.title: Q48. How do you handle a runtime alert at 3am?
docs.text: Runbook: confirm not noise, isolate pod (NetworkPolicy deny + cordon node if needed), capture forensics (process tree, fd list, /proc/PID/maps), preserve container fs, page IR lead if confirmed, postmortem within 5 days.

docs.title: Q49. What is zero-trust in K8s terms?
docs.text: Every connection authenticated and authorized regardless of network position. Identity is workload-bound (SPIFFE), not IP-bound. Default-deny everywhere.

docs.title: Q50. Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium for mTLS?
docs.text: Linkerd: simplest, lowest overhead, ambient not yet GA. Istio: most features, ambient mode reduces sidecar cost. Cilium: eBPF mTLS without sidecars, integrates with NetworkPolicy. Pick by org maturity and feature need.

docs.title: Q51. What is the rollout plan?
docs.text: Phase 1: install mesh, enable PERMISSIVE mTLS, observe. Phase 2: enable STRICT per-namespace, fix exceptions. Phase 3: AuthorizationPolicy default-deny per namespace, allowlist intentional traffic. Phase 4: extend to ingress and egress.

docs.title: Q52. What about non-mesh workloads?
docs.text: Mesh egress gateway, sidecar injection by namespace label, accept-no-mesh annotation for legacy with explicit risk acceptance, plan migration with deadline.

docs.title: Q53. How does SPIFFE fit?
docs.text: SPIFFE provides workload identity (SVID) — X.509 or JWT — issued by SPIRE. Mesh uses SVIDs for mTLS. Workloads outside mesh use SPIRE agent to fetch SVID for cross-system auth (e.g. Vault, DB).

docs.title: Q54. How do you authorize at L7?
docs.text: AuthorizationPolicy with method, path, JWT claims. Validate JWT at sidecar via RequestAuthentication. Pass principal to app for fine-grained checks.

docs.title: Q55. What breaks when you turn on STRICT mTLS?
docs.text: Probes from kubelet (allow with PERMISSIVE on probe port or use exec probes), prometheus scraping (use mesh-aware Prom or scrape through sidecar), legacy clients without mTLS, headless services (work but require attention).

docs.title: Q56. How do you observe mesh traffic?
docs.text: Mesh exposes metrics (request rate, error rate, p99) and traces (Jaeger/Tempo). Build SLOs from these. Kiali for topology. Hubble for Cilium.

docs.title: Q57. What is the first step of a compliance program?
docs.text: Scope. Define cardholder data environment (PCI), ePHI systems (HIPAA), or in-scope services (SOC 2). Network segmentation reduces scope dramatically.

docs.title: Q58. How do you implement PCI segmentation in K8s?
docs.text: Dedicated cluster or dedicated namespace + node pool with taints, network policies block all ingress except payment service entry, egress only to PCI-approved endpoints, all logs to a separate SIEM index, all admin via bastion with MFA.

docs.title: Q59. How do you handle HIPAA encryption?
docs.text: At rest: KMS-encrypted etcd, KMS-encrypted PVs, KMS-encrypted object storage. In transit: TLS 1.2+ everywhere, mTLS via mesh, no plaintext intra-cluster.

docs.title: Q60. SOC 2 logging requirements?
docs.text: CC7.2 — monitor system components. Centralized logs with integrity (signed or WORM), retention 1 year, access reviewed quarterly, alerts on detection of unauthorized changes, evidence for auditor.

docs.title: Q61. How do you produce evidence at audit time?
docs.text: Continuous evidence collection: Drata/Vanta/Secureframe pulling from K8s, cloud, IdP, vuln scanner, SIEM. Store as immutable evidence artifacts with timestamps. Auditor gets read-only access.

docs.title: Q62. How do you handle change management for SOC 2?
docs.text: All changes via PR with approval (CC8.1). GitOps enforces this — direct cluster changes denied via RBAC. Emergency change process documented and audited.

docs.title: Q63. What about access reviews?
docs.text: Quarterly: export RBAC bindings, IAM roles, IdP group memberships. Manager attests per direct report. Revoke on no-attestation. Tool: Sailpoint, custom script, or IdP-native review.

docs.title: Q64. How do you prove vulnerability management?
docs.text: Trivy/Snyk in CI, Grype/Trivy continuously against running images, SLA: critical < 7d, high < 30d. Dashboard with MTTR per severity. Auditor sees SLA hit rate.

docs.title: Q65. What are the IR phases?
docs.text: Prepare, Detect, Analyze, Contain, Eradicate, Recover, Lessons Learned. NIST SP 800-61.

docs.title: Q66. What does prepare look like for K8s?
docs.text: Runbooks per scenario, IR team on-call rotation, tabletop exercises quarterly, forensic tooling pre-installed (sysdig capture, kubectl debug, kube-forensics), evidence pipeline tested, legal/PR contacts known.

docs.title: Q67. Compromised pod — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Confirm via Falco/Tetragon evidence. 2) Cordon node. 3) Apply NetworkPolicy deny on pod label. 4) kubectl debug to capture process list, network conns, env. 5) Snapshot container fs. 6) Delete pod, evict node, rotate any creds it held. 7) Hunt for lateral movement via audit log.

docs.title: Q68. Stolen kubeconfig — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Revoke client cert via CSR deletion or rotate cluster CA (worst case). 2) Disable IdP user. 3) Audit log search for user actions. 4) Inventory created/modified resources, treat as compromised. 5) Rotate any secrets accessed. 6) Postmortem on how it leaked.

docs.title: Q69. Cryptojacking detected — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Kill pod, isolate node. 2) Trace image to source — was it pulled from public registry without verification? 3) Block image digest at admission. 4) Check for persistence (DaemonSets, CronJobs, mutating webhooks). 5) Audit all images deployed since the bad pull.

docs.title: Q70. Ransomware on PV — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Snapshot PV before any action. 2) Identify infection vector (vuln, creds, supply chain). 3) Restore from clean backup to new namespace. 4) Validate backup integrity before cutover. 5) Rotate all creds in scope. 6) Notify per legal/regulatory requirements (HIPAA 60d, GDPR 72h).

docs.title: Q71. Public exposure of S3-equivalent / etcd snapshot — playbook?
docs.text: 1) Lock down ACL immediately. 2) Determine what data was exposed and for how long via access logs. 3) Notify legal. 4) Rotate any credentials/PII keys in the exposed data. 5) Postmortem on bucket policy gap, IaC guardrail to prevent recurrence.

docs.title: Q72. How do you measure IR maturity?
docs.text: MTTD (mean time to detect), MTTR (respond), MTTC (contain), tabletop frequency, runbook coverage of scenarios, % of detections with auto-containment, postmortem completion rate.

docs.title: Closing principles
docs.text:
• Default-deny everything: network, RBAC, admission, egress.
  • Identity is the new perimeter: SPIFFE for workloads, OIDC for humans.
  • Sign and verify everything: image, attestation, config bundle.
  • Detect at runtime — preventive controls fail.
  • Practice IR before you need it.
  • Evidence is continuous, not annual.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference of common DevOps, Kubernetes, container, and platform terms used throughout this site. Hover any abbreviation in the docs to see its definition (when supported by the browser).

docs.title: Security for 10-Year-Olds (ELI10)
docs.text: Security stuff explained like you're 10. Each idea has an analogy, the real thing, a tiny diagram, and commands you can actually run.

docs.title: 1. RBAC = different keys for different rooms
Analogy
docs.text: Imagine a school. The art teacher has a key to the art room. The science teacher has a key to the science lab. The principal has a master key. Nobody walks around with every key — that would be dangerous if they lost it.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) gives each person or robot a small set of permissions. A "Role" is the keyring. A "RoleBinding" hands the keyring to someone.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User]
  RB[RoleBinding]
  R[Role]
  K[API Resources]
  U --> RB --> R --> K

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Make a role that can only read pods
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list --resource=pods -n demo

# Give it to a user
kubectl create rolebinding read-pods --role=pod-reader --user=alice -n demo

# Check what alice can do
kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=alice -n demo   # yes
kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as=alice -n demo # no

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Never make someone cluster-admin "just for now". That's the master key. They'll keep it forever.

docs.title: 2. NetworkPolicy = list of friends who can talk to you
Analogy
docs.text: You're at lunch. You have a rule: only kids from your class can sit at your table. Everyone else has to sit somewhere else. That rule is a NetworkPolicy.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: NetworkPolicy says: "pods with this label can receive traffic only from pods with that label, on these ports." Without one, every pod talks to every pod.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  F[Frontend]
  B[Backend]
  D[Database]
  F --> B --> D

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Default deny: nobody talks to anyone in the namespace
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: demo
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
EOF

# Allow frontend to call backend
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: front-to-back
  namespace: demo
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: backend }
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels: { app: frontend }
    ports:
    - port: 8080
EOF

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: You need a CNI that supports NetworkPolicy (Calico, Cilium). On a CNI that ignores it, the rules do nothing — silently.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: Your diary has a tiny lock. You write your feelings inside. Your sister can see the diary on the shelf, but she cannot read it without the key. The key is hidden.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: A Secret holds passwords or tokens. K8s base64-encodes it (not secure!) and stores it. Encryption-at-rest in etcd is the real lock.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  P[Pod]
  V[Volume]
  S[Secret]
  K[KMS]
  P --> V --> S --> K

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Make a secret
kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=password=hunter2 -n demo

# Mount and read it
kubectl run app -n demo --image=busybox --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl set volume pod/app -n demo --add --name=pwd --type=secret --secret-name=db-pass --mount-path=/etc/db
kubectl exec -n demo app -- cat /etc/db/password

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Never put a Secret in a git repo as plain YAML. Use SealedSecrets or External Secrets.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: Two friends in a club have a secret handshake. When one walks up, they do the handshake. If you don't know the handshake, you don't get in. And both sides check — it's not just a one-way thing.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: mTLS (mutual TLS) means both server and client show certificates. The server proves it's the real server. The client proves it's an allowed client. A service mesh does this for every pod-to-pod call automatically.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  A[Pod A]
  SA[Sidecar A]
  SB[Sidecar B]
  B[Pod B]
  A --> SA --> SB --> B

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Install Linkerd (simplest mesh)
linkerd install --crds | kubectl apply -f -
linkerd install | kubectl apply -f -

# Inject sidecars into a namespace
kubectl annotate ns demo linkerd.io/inject=enabled

# Roll deployments to pick up the sidecar
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n demo

# See the traffic with mTLS
linkerd viz tap deploy/frontend -n demo

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Probes from kubelet are not in the mesh. Either use exec probes or allow probe traffic to bypass.

docs.title: 5. Admission webhook = bouncer at the door
Analogy
docs.text: A nightclub has a bouncer. Before you go in, the bouncer checks your ID, your shoes, your shirt. If anything's off, you don't get in. The bouncer can also hand you a wristband (mutate you) before letting you through.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: A ValidatingWebhook says yes/no to every API request. A MutatingWebhook can change the request before it's stored. OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno are popular bouncers.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  K[kubectl apply]
  API[API Server]
  W[Webhook]
  ETC[etcd]
  K --> API --> W --> ETC

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Install Kyverno
kubectl create -f https://github.com/kyverno/kyverno/releases/latest/download/install.yaml

# Block any pod without resource limits
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: { name: require-limits }
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-limits
    match:
      any:
      - resources: { kinds: [Pod] }
    validate:
      message: Containers must set resource limits.
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - resources:
              limits: { memory: ?*, cpu: ?* }
EOF
kubectl run nolimit --image=nginx   # should fail

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Webhook down = API server slow or stuck. Always set failurePolicy: Ignore for non-critical, Fail only for must-have.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: You buy cookies at the store. The bag has a special seal. If someone opened it and put in something gross, the seal would be broken and you'd see. Also there's a sticker that says which factory made them.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) attaches signed proof (provenance) to every build. You can verify "this image was built by our trusted CI from this source commit, nothing else."

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  S[Source]
  CI[CI Builder]
  IMG[Image]
  PROV[Provenance]
  REG[Registry]
  S --> CI --> IMG --> REG
  CI --> PROV --> REG

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Sign keylessly with sigstore (uses your OIDC token)
cosign sign registry/myapp:v1

# Generate SBOM and attach as attestation
syft registry/myapp:v1 -o spdx-json > sbom.json
cosign attest --predicate sbom.json --type spdx registry/myapp:v1

# Verify before deploy
cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp=.*@mycompany.com \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://accounts.google.com registry/myapp:v1

# Scan for known holes
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry/myapp:v1

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: A signature only proves who signed it, not that the contents are good. Pair signing with vuln scanning and policy.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: The playground has rules. No running with scissors. No climbing the fence. No bringing matches. Some kids get a pass for the woodshop (they can use sharp things) but the regular playground has strict rules.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: Pod Security Admission has three levels: privileged (anything goes — woodshop), baseline (no scissors), restricted (no scissors, no matches, helmet on). Apply per namespace.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  NS[Namespace]
  L[Label]
  PSA[PSA Controller]
  POD[Pod]
  NS --> L --> PSA --> POD

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
# Lock down a namespace
kubectl label ns demo pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted

# Try a privileged pod (should be denied)
kubectl run -n demo bad --image=nginx --privileged

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: restricted requires non-root, seccomp, dropped caps. Many off-the-shelf images break. Test before enforcing.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: A food inspector visits the bakery and checks every batch for problems before it ships to stores. If they find mold, they don't let it ship.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: Trivy or Grype scans container images for known vulnerable libraries (CVEs). You run it in CI to fail bad builds and at runtime to find new problems in already-deployed images.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  IMG[Image]
  SC[Scanner]
  DB[CVE Database]
  REP[Report]
  IMG --> SC --> REP
  DB --> SC

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
trivy image nginx:1.21
grype nginx:1.21
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 nginx:1.21   # fail CI on critical

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: A scanner can only find what its database knows. Update the DB daily. Zero-day vulns are invisible.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: At a big office, every worker wears a badge. The badge has their name, what team they're on, and what floors they can visit. Robots (workloads) need badges too.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: SPIFFE gives each workload a verifiable identity (SVID), like spiffe://company/ns/payments/sa/api. SPIRE issues and rotates these automatically.

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  W[Workload]
  AG[SPIRE Agent]
  SR[SPIRE Server]
  ID[SVID]
  W --> AG --> SR
  SR --> ID --> W

docs.title: Try it
docs.text: kubectl exec -n demo app -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-agent api fetch x509

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: SPIRE setup is non-trivial. Most teams get SPIFFE for free via Istio or Linkerd.

docs.title: Analogy
docs.text: Your house has motion sensors. If someone breaks a window or sneaks in at night, the alarm goes off. You can't prevent every break-in, but you can know fast.

docs.title: Real thing
docs.text: Falco watches every process, file, and network event in your cluster. Rules say "alert if someone runs a shell inside a container."

docs.title: Diagram
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  K[Kernel]
  F[Falco]
  R[Rules]
  AL[Alert]
  K --> F --> AL
  R --> F

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
helm install falco falcosecurity/falco -n falco --create-namespace
kubectl run shell --image=busybox -- sh -c 'sleep 600'
kubectl exec shell -- sh
kubectl logs -n falco -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco --tail=20

docs.title: Trap
docs.text: Default rules will be noisy. Plan a tuning sprint in week two.

docs.title: What to do next
docs.text:
1. Run all the commands in a throwaway kind/minikube cluster.
  2. Open visual-flows.md to see how requests travel through these pieces.
  3. Read architect-qa.md when you start designing for a real org.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: A reference of common DevOps, Kubernetes, container, and platform terms used throughout this site. Hover any abbreviation in the docs to see its definition (when supported by the browser).

docs.title: Visual Flows — Security
docs.text: 10 simple mermaid flowcharts showing how requests, decisions, and trust flow through Kubernetes and cloud-native security systems. Each chart has a brief explanation, follow-up notes, and the relevant kubectl/cosign commands.

docs.title: 1. kubectl request — authn to authz to admission to etcd
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  U[User]
  AN[Authn]
  AZ[Authz]
  AD[Admission]
  ETC[etcd]
  U --> AN --> AZ --> AD --> ETC

The full path of any kubectl apply. Authn proves who you are (cert, token, OIDC). Authz checks RBAC. Admission validates and mutates. Then store.

Failure modes - Authn fails: 401 Unauthorized - Authz fails: 403 Forbidden - Admission denies: webhook error message - etcd unavailable: 500

Commands 

kubectl auth whoami
kubectl auth can-i create pods -n demo
kubectl get --raw /api/v1/namespaces/demo/pods --v=8

docs.title: 2. RBAC authorization decision
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  REQ[Request]
  RB[RoleBinding]
  R[Role]
  V[Verb Check]
  D[Decision]
  REQ --> RB --> R --> V --> D

Every request maps to subject + verb + resource. RBAC walks every (Cluster)RoleBinding for the subject and unions the rules.

Default: deny. Explicit allow required.

Commands 

kubectl auth can-i --list --as=system:serviceaccount:demo:app
kubectl get clusterrolebindings -o wide | grep alice
kubectl describe role pod-reader -n demo

docs.title: 3. Admission policy decision (Kyverno or Gatekeeper)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  AR[AdmissionReview]
  POL[Policy]
  EV[Evaluate]
  RES[Result]
  ETC[etcd]
  AR --> POL --> EV --> RES --> ETC

API server sends AdmissionReview to webhook. Policy engine evaluates against rules. Allow/deny/mutate returned.

Failure policy decides what happens if the webhook is unreachable: Ignore (allow) or Fail (deny).

Commands 

kubectl get clusterpolicies
kubectl get policyreports -A
kubectl get validatingwebhookconfigurations

docs.title: 4. NetworkPolicy traffic decision
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  SRC[Source Pod]
  CNI[CNI]
  POL[Policy Match]
  DEC[Decision]
  DST[Dest Pod]
  SRC --> CNI --> POL --> DEC --> DST

CNI evaluates ingress/egress rules per pod label. Default = allow if no policy targets the pod, deny if any policy selects it (without matching the rule).

Common pattern: apply default-deny to namespace, then allowlist intentional flows.

Commands 

kubectl get netpol -A
kubectl describe netpol default-deny -n demo
kubectl exec -n demo client -- nc -zv backend 8080

docs.title: 5. Image signing flow (cosign keyless)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  DEV[CI Build]
  OIDC[OIDC Token]
  FUL[Fulcio CA]
  CRT[Short Cert]
  SIG[Signed Image]
  DEV --> OIDC --> FUL --> CRT --> SIG

CI presents OIDC identity to Fulcio, gets a short-lived signing certificate, signs the image. Signature stored in registry next to image. Rekor logs the event for transparency.

Commands 

cosign sign registry/app:v1
cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp=.*@company.com \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  registry/app:v1

docs.title: 6. Image admission verification
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod Spec]
  AD[Admission Webhook]
  COS[Cosign Verify]
  REG[Registry]
  DEC[Allow or Deny]
  POD --> AD --> COS --> REG
  COS --> DEC

Sigstore policy controller (or Kyverno verifyImages) intercepts pod creates, fetches signature from registry, verifies against allowed identity, allows only if signed by expected builder.

Commands 

kubectl get clusterimagepolicies
kubectl run unsigned --image=docker.io/random/unverified

docs.title: 7. Secret pull from external store (External Secrets Operator)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  ES[ExternalSecret]
  SS[SecretStore]
  VLT[Vault]
  K8S[K8s Secret]
  POD[Pod]
  ES --> SS --> VLT --> K8S --> POD

ExternalSecret references a SecretStore which holds connection + auth to Vault/AWS SM/etc. ESO polls or watches, writes a native K8s Secret, pod consumes via volume.

Commands 

kubectl get externalsecrets -A
kubectl describe externalsecret app-creds -n demo
vault kv get secret/demo/app

docs.title: 8. SPIFFE attestation flow
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  POD[Workload]
  AGT[SPIRE Agent]
  ATT[Attest]
  SRV[SPIRE Server]
  SVID[X509 SVID]
  POD --> AGT --> ATT --> SRV --> SVID

Agent on each node attests workload (via k8s_psat selector: namespace, SA, image). Server issues SVID. Workload uses SVID for mTLS or to authenticate to Vault, DB, mesh.

Commands 

kubectl exec -n demo app -- /opt/spire/bin/spire-agent api fetch x509
kubectl logs -n spire spire-server-0

docs.title: 9. OIDC token exchange (workload to AWS via IRSA)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  POD[Pod with SA]
  TOK[Projected Token]
  STS[AWS STS]
  ROLE[IAM Role]
  CRED[Temp Creds]
  POD --> TOK --> STS --> ROLE --> CRED

Pod has a projected SA token (audience = sts.amazonaws.com). SDK calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AWS validates token signature against cluster OIDC issuer JWKS, returns 1h credentials.

Commands 

kubectl get sa app -n demo -o yaml
aws sts get-caller-identity
aws iam get-role --role-name eks-demo-app

docs.title: 10. Runtime detection alert pipeline
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  K[Kernel Events]
  EBP[eBPF Probe]
  RU[Rule Engine]
  SK[Sidekick]
  SIEM[SIEM Alert]
  K --> EBP --> RU --> SK --> SIEM

Falco/Tetragon hooks kernel via eBPF, evaluates rules in userspace (Falco) or in-kernel (Tetragon), forwards to falcosidekick which routes to SIEM, Slack, PagerDuty.

Commands 

kubectl logs -n falco -l app.kubernetes.io/name=falco --tail=100
tetra getevents -o compact
curl -s http://falcosidekick:2801/healthz

docs.title: How to use these diagrams
docs.text:
• During design reviews, draw the flow for the proposed change. If you can't, the design is incomplete.
  • During incidents, the flow tells you where to look. A 403 means stop at step 2 of flow 1.
  • When teaching, walk left-to-right for each flow before showing YAML.

docs.title: Combined trust chain (everything together)
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
  SRC[Source]
  CI[CI Build]
  REG[Registry]
  AD[Admission]
  POD[Pod]
  MESH[Mesh]
  SRC --> CI --> REG --> AD --> POD --> MESH

End-to-end: code goes to CI, CI builds and signs image, registry stores image plus signature plus attestations, admission verifies signature and policy at deploy, pod runs with workload identity and mTLS via mesh.

docs.title: Failure mapping
docs.text: Symptom Likely flow Where to look 401 from kubectl Flow 1 step 2 IdP, kubeconfig, cert expiry 403 from kubectl Flow 2 RBAC bindings for subject Pod denied at create Flow 3 or 6 webhook logs, policy reports Pod cannot reach service Flow 4 netpol describe, CNI logs Image rejected Flow 6 cosign verify locally Secret missing Flow 7 ExternalSecret status, store auth Cannot assume role Flow 9 STS errors, OIDC provider thumbprint No alerts firing Flow 10 falco pod healthy, sidekick reachable

docs.title: Suggested practice
docs.text:
Pick one flow per week. Draw it from memory on a whiteboard. Then run the commands to confirm each step is healthy in your cluster. After ten weeks, you can debug any security incident by mentally walking the flow.

docs.title: 09 — Terraform: Infrastructure as Code
docs.text: Goal: Take a DevOps learner from zero IaC experience to multi-cloud Terraform proficiency. Every chapter ships runnable .tf files. Early labs need no cloud credentials — they use random, null_resource, and local_file providers.

docs.title: What is Infrastructure as Code (IaC)?
docs.text:
IaC means describing your infrastructure (servers, networks, databases, IAM, K8s clusters) as declarative code that lives in git, gets reviewed in PRs, and is applied by automation — not by clicking around a cloud console.

Benefits: - Reproducible — same code → same infra in dev/staging/prod - Auditable — every change is a git commit - Versioned — rollback is git revert + terraform apply - Collaborative — code review for infra changes - Drift detection — terraform plan shows real vs desired state

docs.title: Terraform vs OpenTofu vs Pulumi
docs.text:
Feature Terraform OpenTofu Pulumi Language HCL (DSL) HCL (DSL) Real languages (TS, Python, Go, C#) License BSL 1.1 (since v1.6) MPL 2.0 (true OSS) Apache 2.0 Provider ecosystem Largest Same registry as TF Smaller but growing State backend S3/GCS/Azure/TFC S3/GCS/Azure/local Pulumi Cloud / S3 CLI compatibility terraform drop-in tofu replacement pulumi (different UX) Best for Industry standard Open-source purists Devs who hate DSLs

Recommendation: Learn Terraform first (largest community, most jobs). OpenTofu is a near-identical fork — your skills transfer. Pulumi is a separate skill.

docs.title: High-level workflow
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[Write .tf files] --> B[terraform initdownloads providers]
    B --> C[terraform planshows diff]
    C --> D{Looks good?}
    D -->|yes| E[terraform applycreates/updates infra]
    D -->|no| A
    E --> F[(terraform.tfstatetracks reality)]
    F --> C
    E --> G[terraform destroytear down]

docs.title: Course Map
docs.text: Chapter Topic Cloud creds? 01-install Install Terraform / OpenTofu No 02-hello-world First init/plan/apply No 03-language-basics HCL syntax deep-dive No 04-providers Provider model & versioning No 05-variables-outputs Inputs / outputs / tfvars No 06-state Local & remote state, locking Optional 07-modules Modules: build & consume No 08-workspaces-and-environments dev/staging/prod patterns No 09-aws-examples S3, VPC, EKS Yes (AWS) 10-gcp-examples GCS, GKE Yes (GCP) 11-kubernetes-provider TF for K8s + Helm Kube context 12-testing fmt, validate, tflint, tfsec, terraform test No 13-cicd GitHub Actions + OIDC Yes (in CI) 14-best-practices Production patterns No cheatsheet.md Command reference —

docs.title: Quick install (mac)
docs.text:
brew install terraform        # or: brew install opentofu
terraform version

See 01-install for Linux, Windows, and tfenv (multi-version manager).

docs.title: How to use this course
docs.text:
1. Read each chapter's README.md first.
  2. cd into the chapter folder, run terraform init && terraform plan && terraform apply.
  3. Inspect terraform.tfstate (don't commit it!).
  4. Run terraform destroy to clean up before moving on.
  5. Take notes in your own learnings.md.

Rule #1: never commit *.tfstate, *.tfstate.backup, .terraform/, or *.tfvars files containing secrets. A .gitignore template lives in 14-best-practices.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
terraform init                  # download providers, init backend
terraform init -upgrade         # upgrade provider versions
terraform init -migrate-state   # move state between backends
terraform fmt -recursive        # format .tf files

docs.title: 02 — Hello, Terraform
docs.text: Your first lab. No cloud credentials needed — we'll generate a random pet name and write it to a local file.

docs.title: Files
docs.text: • main.tf — uses random + local_file providers.

docs.title: The five commands you'll run forever
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as You
    participant TF as terraform CLI
    participant R as Provider Registry
    participant S as State (local file)
    participant W as World (cloud / disk)

    U->>TF: terraform init
    TF->>R: download providers
    TF-->>U: ready
    U->>TF: terraform plan
    TF->>S: read current state
    TF->>W: refresh real-world status
    TF-->>U: diff (create / update / destroy)
    U->>TF: terraform apply
    TF->>W: apply changes
    TF->>S: update state
    TF-->>U: outputs
    U->>TF: terraform destroy
    TF->>W: tear down
    TF->>S: clear state

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
cd 02-hello-world
terraform init       # downloads random + local providers
terraform plan       # shows: 2 to add
terraform apply      # type 'yes'
cat hello.txt        # → "Hello from <random-pet-name>"
terraform destroy    # type 'yes'

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
1. A random_pet resource (e.g. clever-otter).
  2. A local_file resource that writes hello.txt on disk.

docs.title: What you'll see on disk after apply
docs.text:
.terraform/                      ← provider plugins (don't commit)
.terraform.lock.hcl              ← provider version lockfile (DO commit)
hello.txt                        ← the file we created
terraform.tfstate                ← current state (DON'T commit)
terraform.tfstate.backup         ← previous state

See walkthrough.md for a line-by-line explanation.

docs.title: Block 1 — terraform { ... }
docs.text:
Top-level settings for the configuration itself (not for any resource): - required_version — pins the minimum Terraform CLI version. - required_providers — declares which providers (and which versions) this config uses. Terraform downloads these during init.

Pinning prevents "works on my machine" — your team gets the exact same plugin versions.

docs.title: Block 2 — resource "random_pet" "name" { ... }
docs.text:
• random_pet — the resource type (defined by the random provider).
  • name — your local label for this resource. Used to reference it elsewhere as random_pet.name.
  • length, separator — arguments specific to this resource type.

Every resource has a unique id. For random_pet, the id is the generated name.

docs.title: Block 3 — resource "local_file" "hello" { ... }
docs.text: • Interpolation: ${random_pet.name.id} reads the output of the previous resource. Terraform uses these references to build a dependency graph — local_file will always be created after random_pet.

docs.title: Block 4 — output { ... }
docs.text: Outputs surface values to the CLI and to other configs (when used as a module). Run terraform output to view them after apply.

docs.title: Lifecycle on each command
docs.text: Command Effect init Downloads hashicorp/random and hashicorp/local plugins into .terraform/, writes .terraform.lock.hcl. plan Builds DAG, computes diff. First run: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. apply Executes the plan. random_pet first → its output flows into local_file. State written. apply (again, no changes) 0 to add — Terraform is idempotent. Edit length = 3, apply random_pet is replaced (regenerates name) → local_file updates with new content. destroy Deletes hello.txt, removes both resources from state.

docs.title: Try this
docs.text:
1. Change length = 2 to length = 4. Run plan — note the ~ (in-place) vs -/+ (replace) markers.
  2. Add a second local_file resource that writes the name in uppercase: content = upper(random_pet.name.id).
  3. Run terraform graph | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg to visualize the dependency graph.

docs.title: 03 — HCL Language Basics
docs.text: HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL2) is a declarative DSL. You describe what you want; Terraform figures out how.

docs.title: The five core constructs
docs.text: Construct Purpose Example Block Named container resource "aws_s3_bucket" "x" { ... } Argument name = value inside a block bucket = "my-data" Expression Produces a value var.env, "prefix-${var.name}", [for x in list : x*2] Type string, number, bool, list, set, map, object, tuple list(string), map(number) Meta-argument Modifies any resource count, for_each, depends_on, provider, lifecycle

docs.title: Mermaid: how a configuration is evaluated
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart TD
    A[Parse .tf files] --> B[Build resource graph]
    B --> C[Resolve variableslocals, data sources]
    C --> D[Evaluate expressionsfor/for_each/dynamic]
    D --> E[Compute desired state]
    E --> F[Diff vs current state]
    F --> G[Plan output]

docs.title: Looping: count vs for_each
docs.text:
• count = 3 → creates indexed resources (aws_instance.web[0], [1], [2]). Use for identical copies.
  • for_each = toset([...]) or for_each = { ... } → creates keyed resources. Use when items have different identities (safer — adding/removing one item won't reshuffle the others).

docs.title: for expressions
docs.text:
locals {
  upper_names = [for n in var.names : upper(n)]
  by_id       = { for u in var.users : u.id => u.name }
  evens       = [for x in range(10) : x if x % 2 == 0]
}

docs.title: dynamic blocks
docs.text:
Generate nested blocks programmatically: 

resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  dynamic "ingress" {
    for_each = var.allowed_ports
    content {
      from_port   = ingress.value
      to_port     = ingress.value
      protocol    = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
    }
  }
}

docs.text: instance_type = var.env == "prod" ? "m5.large" : "t3.small"

docs.title: 04 — Providers
docs.text: A provider is a plugin that talks to an API (AWS, GCP, Kubernetes, GitHub, Datadog, even your local filesystem). Providers define resource types and data sources.

docs.title: Provider registry
docs.text:
• Public: https://registry.terraform.io
  • OpenTofu mirror: https://search.opentofu.org
  • You can also host private providers (Terraform Cloud, Artifactory, etc.).

docs.title: required_providers
docs.text:
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5.0"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"     # registry namespace/name
      version = "~> 5.0"            # version constraint
    }
    google = {
      source  = "hashicorp/google"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
    kubernetes = {
      source  = "hashicorp/kubernetes"
      version = "~> 2.30"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Version constraint operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning Example = Exact = 5.20.0 != Exclude != 5.19.0 >=, <=, >, < Comparison >= 5.0.0 ~> Pessimistic — last component may bump ~> 5.0 = >= 5.0, < 6.0; ~> 5.20.0 = >= 5.20.0, < 5.21.0

Best practice: pin the major version with ~> (e.g. ~> 5.0) and rely on .terraform.lock.hcl for exact reproducibility.

docs.title: Provider configuration
docs.text:
provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

Auth comes from env vars / shared config files / IAM roles — never hardcode credentials in .tf files.

docs.title: Multiple providers via alias
docs.text:
Use the same provider with different configs (multi-region, multi-account):

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "us"
  region = "us-east-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "eu_logs" {
  bucket = "eu-logs"
  # uses default provider
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "us_logs" {
  provider = aws.us
  bucket   = "us-logs"
}

docs.title: Mermaid: provider resolution flow
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
flowchart LR
    A[terraform init] --> B[Read required_providers]
    B --> C[Resolve via registry]
    C --> D[Download plugin to .terraform/]
    D --> E[Write .terraform.lock.hcl]
    E --> F[plan/apply uses cached plugin]
    F --> G[Plugin -> Cloud API]

docs.title: Lockfile (.terraform.lock.hcl)
docs.text:
• Records the exact provider version + checksum used.
  • Commit it. Ensures CI and teammates use the same plugin.
  • Update with terraform init -upgrade.

docs.title: Useful first-party providers (no cloud creds)
docs.text:
Provider Use hashicorp/random Random strings, IDs, passwords hashicorp/local Read/write local files hashicorp/null null_resource for orchestration / local-exec hashicorp/time Sleeps, timestamps, rotating values hashicorp/tls Generate self-signed certs / private keys hashicorp/http HTTP GET as a data source

  -platform=darwin_arm64 \

docs.title: Input variables
docs.text:
Inputs make a config reusable. Declare them once, override per environment.

variable "env" {
  type        = string
  description = "Environment name."
  default     = "dev"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.env)
    error_message = "env must be one of: dev, staging, prod."
  }
}

docs.title: Type constraints
docs.text:
type = string
type = number
type = bool
type = list(string)
type = set(string)
type = map(number)
type = object({ name = string, port = number })
type = tuple([string, number, bool])

docs.title: Sensitive variables
docs.text:
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
Sensitive values are masked in CLI output but still written to state — protect your state file.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
output "bucket_arn" {
  value       = aws_s3_bucket.demo.arn
  description = "ARN of the data bucket."
  sensitive   = false
}
Outputs are visible after apply and are how modules expose values to callers.

docs.title: Variable input precedence (low → high)
docs.text:
1. Defaults in variable {} blocks
  2. terraform.tfvars (auto-loaded)
  3. *.auto.tfvars (auto-loaded, alphabetical)
  4. -var-file=... CLI flag
  5. -var name=value CLI flag
  6. TF_VAR_<name> environment variable
Mermaid source 
flowchart TD
    A[variable default] --> B[terraform.tfvars]
    B --> C[*.auto.tfvars]
    C --> D[-var-file CLI]
    D --> E[-var CLI]
    E --> F[TF_VAR_* env]
    F --> G[Final value]

docs.title: Variables & Outputs — Commands
docs.text: Quick pickup reference. Pair with README.md for theory.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
cd 05-variables-outputs
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
# Edit terraform.tfvars to fit your project
terraform fmt

docs.title: Init / plan / apply
docs.text:
terraform init

# Defaults only (uses the var defaults baked into variables.tf)
terraform plan

# tfvars file (auto-loaded if named terraform.tfvars or *.auto.tfvars)
terraform plan -var-file=terraform.tfvars

# Inline override on the CLI (highest precedence among flags)
terraform plan -var="env=staging" -var="instance_count=4"

# Environment variable wins over tfvars
TF_VAR_env=staging terraform plan
TF_VAR_db_password='supersecret' terraform apply -auto-approve

# Multiple var files (later files override earlier ones)
terraform apply -var-file=base.tfvars -var-file=prod.auto.tfvars

docs.title: State operations
docs.text:
terraform state list

# Outputs are stored in state — inspect them
terraform state pull | jq '.outputs'

docs.title: Inspect / verify
docs.text:
# Read all outputs after apply
terraform output
terraform output resource_prefix
terraform output -raw resource_prefix          # unquoted, for scripts
terraform output -json merged_tags | jq .
terraform output -json public_subnets | jq .

# Sensitive output is masked in the table view; force-show:
terraform output db_password_redacted          # <sensitive>
terraform output -raw db_password_redacted     # actual value (be careful)

# Try a variable validation rule live
terraform plan -var="project_name=BadName"     # fails the regex validation
terraform plan -var="instance_count=99"        # fails the 1..10 validation

# Test variable type coercion in console
terraform console
> var.subnet_config["a"].cidr_block
> [for k, v in var.subnet_config : k if v.public]

docs.title: Cleanup (destroy)
docs.text:
terraform destroy -auto-approve
rm -f terraform.tfvars            # remove only if it held real secrets
rm -rf .terraform terraform.tfstate*

docs.title: One-liners worth memorising
docs.text:
# All-from-env: feed every variable from the shell
export TF_VAR_project_name=demo TF_VAR_env=dev TF_VAR_db_password=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
terraform apply -auto-approve

# Pipe outputs into other tools
export BUCKET=$(terraform output -raw resource_prefix)
aws s3 ls "s3://${BUCKET}-data/"

# Show the resolved value of every variable without applying
terraform console <<<'var'

# Force-rebuild the auto-loaded var file in CI
terraform plan -var-file="envs/${ENV}.tfvars" -out=tfplan

docs.title: 06 — State
docs.text:
Terraform's state maps your config to real-world resources. It's a JSON file (terraform.tfstate) that records "resource aws_s3_bucket.demo corresponds to AWS bucket ID xyz, with these attributes".

Without state, Terraform has no way to know what it created last time → it would either re-create everything or do nothing.

docs.title: Local vs remote state
docs.text: Local Remote Where terraform.tfstate on your laptop S3 / GCS / Azure Blob / Terraform Cloud Multi-user ❌ conflicts ✅ shared Locking ❌ ✅ (DynamoDB / native) Secrets exposure On every dev's laptop Encrypted at rest Production-ready No Yes — always use remote state in prod

docs.title: State locking — why it matters
docs.text:
Mermaid source 
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Dev A
    participant B as Dev B
    participant L as Lock Table (DynamoDB)
    participant S as State (S3)

    A->>L: acquire lock (LockID=demo)
    L-->>A: OK
    A->>S: read state
    B->>L: acquire lock
    L-->>B: BUSY (held by A)
    A->>S: write state
    A->>L: release lock
    B->>L: acquire lock
    L-->>B: OK
    B->>S: read latest state

Without locking, two applys in parallel can corrupt state.

docs.title: Backend types
docs.text: Backend Locking via Notes local OS file lock Default. Single user only. s3 DynamoDB table Most common in AWS shops. gcs Native (GCS object versioning + lock) Most common in GCP. azurerm Native (blob lease) Azure Storage Account. remote (Terraform Cloud) TFC service Free tier exists; nicest UX. http HTTP API GitLab managed state, etc.

docs.title: Example: S3 + DynamoDB
docs.text:
See backend-s3.tf. One-time setup (chicken-and-egg — create the bucket and table outside TF, or with a bootstrap config that uses local state): 

aws s3 mb s3://my-tf-state-prod --region eu-west-1
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket my-tf-state-prod \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name tf-locks \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=LockID,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=LockID,KeyType=HASH \
  --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST --region eu-west-1

docs.title: Migrating local → remote
docs.text:
# 1. Add backend block to your config
# 2. Re-init; TF detects the change and offers to copy
terraform init -migrate-state

docs.title: State surgery — when things go wrong
docs.text: Command Purpose terraform state list List all tracked resources. terraform state show <addr> Inspect attributes. terraform state mv <src> <dst> Rename without destroy/recreate (e.g. after refactoring). terraform state rm <addr> Forget a resource (does NOT delete it in cloud). terraform import <addr> <id> Bring an existing cloud resource under TF management. terraform refresh Sync state with reality (no changes applied). terraform state pull Dump remote state to stdout. terraform state push Upload edited state (dangerous!).

docs.title: Golden rules
docs.text:
1. Never edit terraform.tfstate by hand.
  2. Always back it up before surgery (terraform state pull > backup.tfstate).
  3. Never commit state to git — it contains plaintext secrets.
  4. Always enable state locking in production.
  5. Always enable bucket versioning on the state backend (point-in-time recovery).

docs.text: Quick pickup reference. Pair with README.md for theory.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
cd 06-state
ls                 # backend-s3.tf, backend-gcs.tf, README.md

# Bootstrap S3 + DynamoDB (one-time, out-of-band)
aws s3 mb s3://my-tf-state-prod --region eu-west-1
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket my-tf-state-prod \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=LockID,AttributeType=S \

# GCS backend bootstrap

docs.title: Init / plan / apply
docs.text:
# First init against a remote backend
terraform init

# Migrate from local state to a newly-configured remote backend
terraform init -migrate-state

# Re-configure backend (e.g. changed bucket / region) without migrating
terraform init -reconfigure

# Pass backend settings via CLI instead of HCL (CI-friendly)
terraform init \
  -backend-config="bucket=my-tf-state-prod" \
  -backend-config="key=stacks/network/terraform.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=eu-west-1" \
  -backend-config="dynamodb_table=tf-locks"

docs.title: State operations
docs.text:
terraform state list
terraform state show aws_s3_bucket.demo

# Refactoring — rename without destroy/recreate
terraform state mv aws_s3_bucket.old aws_s3_bucket.new
terraform state mv 'module.app.aws_iam_role.x' 'module.platform.aws_iam_role.x'

# Forget a resource (does NOT delete in cloud)
terraform state rm aws_s3_bucket.legacy

# Adopt an existing cloud resource
terraform import aws_s3_bucket.adopted my-existing-bucket-name

# Sync state with reality (no apply)
terraform refresh
terraform apply -refresh-only

# Pull / push raw state
terraform state pull > backup.tfstate
terraform state push edited.tfstate            # DANGEROUS

# Force-release a stuck lock (only after confirming nobody is applying)
terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>

docs.title: Inspect / verify
docs.text:
# Where is the backend configured?
cat .terraform/terraform.tfstate | jq '.backend'

# What's in the remote state right now?
terraform state pull | jq '.resources | length'
terraform state pull | jq '.resources[].type' | sort -u

# Confirm versioning is on (S3)
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket my-tf-state-prod

# Inspect lock table entries (S3 backend)
aws dynamodb scan --table-name tf-locks --region eu-west-1

docs.title: Cleanup (destroy)
docs.text:
# Tear down infra first
terraform destroy -auto-approve

# Then (optionally) the backend itself
aws s3 rm s3://my-tf-state-prod --recursive
aws s3 rb s3://my-tf-state-prod
aws dynamodb delete-table --table-name tf-locks --region eu-west-1

gcloud storage rm -r gs://my-tf-state-prod

docs.title: One-liners worth memorising
docs.text:
# Always back up before surgery
terraform state pull > "backup-$(date +%s).tfstate"

# Spot drift quickly
terraform plan -refresh-only -no-color | grep -E 'will be|forces replacement'

# Move a whole module under a new key
terraform state mv 'module.vpc' 'module.network.module.vpc'

# Re-init pointing at a different workspace's state path
terraform init -backend-config="key=stacks/network/dev/terraform.tfstate" -reconfigure
